endorsements.quote: By limiting the scope to a few institutions, policymakers and clinicians can carefully observe how AI systems perform, gather valuable feedback, and refine integration protocols before broader deployment [ 21 , 23 ].
In the immediate stage, pilot programs focusing on AI-assisted diagnostic tools should be introduced in selected LMIC hospitals.
Combined with open data initiatives (e.g., AfNiA), these methods mitigate the risk of exacerbating health disparities and emphasize local validation instead of relying solely on HIC-trained models.
For example, a model with 99% sensitivity could still miss thousands of cases out of a million scans, highlighting the pressing need for ongoing, post-deployment performance evaluations.

Researchers and policymakers should promote bespoke or fine-tuned AI models—like SAMBA for glioma segmentation—to accommodate regional disease profiles, imaging constraints, and underrepresented demographics [ 12 , 13 ].

Integrating AI education into medical school curricula, radiology residency programs, and continuing professional development courses ensures that clinicians become fluent in both AI fundamentals and practical imaging workflows [ 48 , 49 ].

unlisted_practices: Governments and healthcare institutions should prioritize cost-effective, portable imaging solutions and low-field MRI to expand equitable diagnostic access.
Establish train-the-trainer programs to build self-sustaining local pools of AI experts.
Adopt retention policies such as career advancement pathways and collaborative research opportunities to address health workforce brain drain.
LMIC governments should establish or empower AI regulatory bodies modeled on successful examples to ensure transparency, patient autonomy, and data privacy.
Develop and implement standardized, harmonized AI regulatory frameworks across LMICs.
Establish regional AI research, training, and data hubs to build capacity and share best practices.
Secure sustained long-term financing for AI initiatives through public-private partnerships and global health financing frameworks so projects do not stall after pilots.
Pair every technical AI pilot with a governance compact specifying data ownership, algorithmic audit rights, and benefit-sharing mechanisms.
Co-create AI tools with communities through participatory design that reflects local diagnostic priorities, languages, and risk tolerances.
Build ethically sourced, population-specific imaging datasets using informed consent, anonymization, and transparent community engagement.
Explore synthetic health data to supplement scarce population-specific datasets.
Keep a human-in-the-loop with continuous oversight by a healthcare professional working alongside AI tools.
Adopt a hub-and-spoke pathway of adapting foundation models via federated learning with quarterly re-validation using drift-surveillance dashboards.
Combine AI deployment with infrastructure upgrades and education, integrating AI into local workflows.
Use harmonized imaging protocols together with balanced datasets to mitigate race-related performance disparities.
